tagline: Forested Ouachita valleys link railroad Heavener with former timber towns
intro: Mountain Gateway follows US 59/270 for 22 miles from Heavener to the Arkansas line, winding through forested Ouachita valleys. The paved, two-lane road has steep grades and sharp curves. Oklahoma’s tourism department presents this scenic byway as a route through the Winding Stair Mountain National Recreation Area, with spring wildflowers and neighboring wilderness for walking and riding. Side roads and neighboring scenic byways branch into the heavily forested mountains.

Railroads and mills shaped the places along this drive. Heavener’s railway arrived in 1896; farther south, the settlement later called Stapp began as Thomasville in 1897. King-Ryder Lumber built a mill and a railway connecting Thomasville with other lines at Howe. A later Buschow mill closed in 1932 after its cut-and-move-on timber operations, and Stapp’s post office followed in 1944. Heavener took a different course: Kansas City Southern bought its railway in 1900, then established a roundhouse in 1910 and made the town a division point.

From Heavener, the drive heads south on US 59 toward Stapp. Along the way, Zoe lies just east of US 59/270, with the Black Fork of the Poteau River passing its north side. Beyond Stapp, continue to Page, 5.5 miles west of the Arkansas border, on the combined highways.

moments.title: Heavener
moments.text: Heavener’s post office and station began in boxcars: one became the post office in May 1896 and another the station. That year, the Kansas City, Pittsburg and Gulf Railroad laid tracks through town. Kansas City Southern bought the line in 1900 and added a roundhouse in 1910, making Heavener a division point. Rail work continues here: CPKC operates a major yard, a crew base and a fueling facility. The town lay in the Choctaw Nation’s Moshulatubbee District through Oklahoma statehood in 1907. In 1900 and 1901, a predecessor of the Arkansas Western Railroad added an eastward connection into Arkansas.

moments.title: Stapp
moments.text: Nothing remains of old Stapp, a settlement whose fortunes followed successive sawmills. It began as Thomasville in Indian Territory in 1897, about the time Long-Bell Lumber acquired property here. Its subsidiary King-Ryder built both a mill and the Kingston and Choctaw Valley Railroad to connect with lines at Howe. King-Ryder left about 1901, but other timber operators followed. Reborn as Stapp, the settlement gained a Buschow sawmill and a post office. The mill closed in 1932; the post office lasted until 1944. At its height the settlement held about 1,000 people, but the mill buildings do not survive as a town to explore.

moments.title: Page
moments.text: Page stands on US 59 and 270, 5.5 miles west of the Arkansas border. Its post office opened in Indian Territory on April 6, 1896, taking the name of William C. Page, a prominent Choctaw Indian. At its founding, the community lay in Wade County within the Choctaw Nation’s Apukshunnubbee District.
